identity.name: Kingdom of Luang Phrabang
native_names: ອານາຈັກຫຼວງພຣະບາງ

land.text: the northern part of Lan Xang, which kept Luang Prabang after the partition of 1707

predecessors.note: Formed 1707 'as a result of the split of the' Lan Xang kingdom (Kingdom of Luang Phrabang page); Kitsarat was crowned in that year; Vientiane took the centre (vientiane dossier) and Champasak seceded later.

land.text: the Luang Prabang kingdom east of the Mekong, a protectorate of France from 1893

successors.note: 'The French Protectorate of Laos was officially established, with the administrative capital moved from Luang Prabang to Vientiane' (1893). Siam was forced to cede the lands east of the Mekong after the Franco-Siamese conflict of 13 July - 3 October 1893. The royal house stayed on in Luang Prabang as a protectorate until the Kingdom of Laos of 11 May 1947; Cliopatria draws the land as French Indochina only from 1895, so 1894 would be unclaimed (see notes).

capitals.name: Luang Prabang
capitals.note: Infobox: capital Luang Prabang. The administrative capital of the French protectorate moved to Vientiane in 1893; Luang Prabang stayed the royal seat.

rulers.name: Surinyavong II
rulers.note: Listed 'Burmese vassal, 1768-1788' on the page; the status line has Siam as suzerain from 1778. The list then skips 1789-1791.

rulers.name: Anurutha
rulers.note: Confirmed by Rama I in 1791 (History of Laos page); Siamese occupations 1791-1792 and 179.-2 June 1794.

rulers.name: Manthaturath
rulers.note: A monk in Bangkok 1825-1826, the kingdom administered by Thai officials.

rulers.name: Oun Kham
rulers.note: Reigned to 1895 on the page; the protectorate began in 1893.

correction.text: the Luang Prabang shape of 1709 from the founding in 1707

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe, 1707-1708: the kingdom 'was formed in 1707 as a result of the split of the' Lan Xang kingdom; Cliopatria's first shape begins in 1709. The 1709 shape applies from the founding.

1709-1733, 160,714 km2: Louangphrabang, Oudômxai, Phôngsali, Houaphan, Xiangkhoang, Bokeo, Louang Namtha, the north of Vientiane province and Xaignabouri (west of the Mekong), with the Sipsong Chau Tai (Lai Châu, Điện Biên, Sơn La, Lào Cai) in Vietnam. The page gives no area or boundary; 'When the kingdom split, Muang Phuan became a tributary state of Luang Prabang' (Xiangkhouang and Houaphan are drawn as direct land; the ledger records the tributary status), and the Sipsong Chau Tai 'had to pay tribute to China, Vietnam, Lan Xang' (Sip Song Chau Tai page), which makes them a tint, not direct land. Infobox area: none.
1734-1737, 160,741 km2: Same outline to a few cells (the western edge moves 0.02 degrees). Reign of Thao Ang (Inthason) 1723-1749 on the page; nothing dated about borders.

1738-1768, 160,851 km2: Same outline, 160,851 km2 (the maximum). Nothing on the pages moves a border between 1738 and the Burmese conquest of March 1765, which was a vassalage, not an annexation: 'Luang Prabang fell to the Burmese in March 1765' and the Lao kingdoms 'then became Burmese vassals in 1765' (Burmese-Siamese War 1765-1767 page).
1769-1774, 160,713 km2: Same outline; Surinyavong II (1768-1788) reigns, a Burmese vassal on the page's ruler list. The Burmese suzerainty is a tint recorded in the konbaung-dynasty ledger.
1775-1777, 160,521 km2: Same outline; no border changes on any page.

1778-1782, 160,741 km2: Same outline, 1778-1782. The infobox status is 'Vassal of Siam (1778-1893)' from 1778; the Siamese suzerainty is a tint recorded by the Siamese dossiers, the land is unchanged.

correction.text: the 1783 shape with Bokeo and Louang Namtha restored to the Luang Prabang kingdom, as before 1783 and after 1889

keyframe_review.note: 1783-1790, 148,096 km2: The shape loses 12,600 km2 on the west (Bokeo 91 to 35 per cent, Louang Namtha 89 to 11) in 1783, the same cells that Cliopatria's Chiangmai row (1783-1852) gains (Bokeo 57 per cent, Louang Namtha 74 per cent). No page opened records the change: the Kingdom of Luang Phrabang page names no loss, and the Kingdom of Chiang Mai and Kawila pages have the Chiang Mai lords taking only Kengtung and Mong Hsat (1802), Chiang Saen (1804) and Mong Yawng (1805), none of them in Laos. It looks like an artifact of Chiangmai's 1783 outline; the correction restores the 1778 outline (and the 1890 one) at confidence 1: unverified, listed under gaps.

1791-1827, 147,905 km2: Same outline over 37 years. The Siamese occupied Luang Prabang in 1791-1792 and again until 2 June 1794 (ruler list), and Manthaturath lived as a monk in Bangkok 1825-1826 'leaving Luang Phra Bang to be administered by Thai officials'; the ledger records the occupations, the land is unchanged. In 1827 Anouvong 'made more direct overtures to Luang Prabang' (Lao rebellion page).
1828-1855, 148,213 km2: Same outline under Manthaturath, Sukha-Söm and Chantharath's first years; Vientiane (the south neighbour) is annexed by Siam in 1828, leaving Luang Prabang its Siamese vassal.
1856-1872, 148,131 km2: Same outline; the Haw wars (1865-1890) begin in this span, without a dated loss of land on the page.
1873-1884, 148,213 km2: Same outline; Oun Kham reigns from 1868.

1885-1889, 147,934 km2: Same outline until the French conquest of the Sipsong Chau Tai: a French consulate was established at Luang Prabang in 1885, the Siamese-French treaty of 7 May 1886 recognised 'Siamese suzerainty' over Luang Prabang, the Black Flags sacked it in 1887, and French protection was accepted on 27 March 1889 'against Siamese protest'. The Sipsong Chau Tai were 'incorporated into the French protectorate of Tonkin ... after 1888', with a treaty with Đèo Văn Trị of Muang Lay on 7 April 1889 (Sip Song Chau Tai page): the shape should lose them in 1889, one year before Cliopatria does. [Reviewer se-01-i, 2026-10-19: the correction that removed the Sipsong Chau Tai for the whole span 1885-1889 contradicted the 1889 loss in the ledger; the shape stands for 1885-1888 and the removal moves to the new keyframe kingdom-of-luang-phrabang_1889.] Fix fx-31 (F178): the keyframe's years are now written out (from 1885, to 1888). Cliopatria's row for this shape runs to 1889, so in 1889 the compiler drew both this shape (with the five Vietnamese provinces, 104 cells shared with sip-song-chau-tai) and kingdom-of-luang-phrabang_1889, which has them removed. The Sip Song Chau Tai page (opened 2026-11-01): the region 'was incorporated into the French protectorate of Tonkin ... after 1888', by Pavie's 'treaty with Dao Van Tri, the White Tai lord of Muang Lay (Lai Chau) on 7 April 1889', and it 'had to pay tribute to China, Vietnam, Lan Xang/ Luang Phrabang'. The one cell Cliopatria's 1890 shape still shares with sip-song-chau-tai is left to the size rule.

correction.text: Cliopatria's 1885 shape unchanged, applying to 1885-1888 only: the Sipsong Chau Tai are incorporated into Tonkin by the treaty of 7 April 1889, drawn from kingdom-of-luang-phrabang_1889

minus.text: the Sipsong Chau Tai: Lai Châu, Điện Biên, Sơn La and the upper Black River (Tai Dam and Tai Khao lords)

correction.text: the 1885 shape without the Sipsong Chau Tai, which pass to the French protectorate of Tonkin on 7 April 1889

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe, 1889 (added by reviewer se-01-i): the Sipsong Chau Tai 'became an autonomous part of the French protectorate of Tonkin ... in 1889' through Pavie's treaty with Deo Van Tri of Muang Lay on 7 April 1889 (Sip Song Chau Tai page), so the 1885 shape loses Lai Chau, Dien Bien, Son La, Lao Cai and Yen Bai from 1889; Cliopatria's 1890 shape follows.

1890-1894, 124,327 km2: The Sipsong Chau Tai (Lai Châu, Điện Biên, Sơn La, Lào Cai, Yên Bái) are out and Bokeo and Louang Namtha back (91 and 89 per cent); the 1889 loss is dated by the Sip Song Chau Tai page. The shape runs to 1894 but the kingdom became a French protectorate in 1893 and the Siamese ceded the east bank on 3 October 1893 (Luang Prabang page); the shape is right to the end of 1893. Cliopatria draws Laos as French Indochina only from 1895.

region.text: Luang Prabang and the Lao north

ledger.note: 1707: Kitsarat is crowned at Luang Prabang and the kingdom is formed. The kingdom 'was formed in 1707 as a result of the split of the' Lan Xang kingdom (Kingdom of Luang Phrabang page, infobox 'Formed: 1707'; the History of Laos page: Lan Xang 'divided into constituent kingdoms in 1707').

region.text: Muang Phuan, the Plain of Jars

ledger.note: 1707: Muang Phuan becomes a tributary of Luang Prabang. 'When the kingdom split, Muang Phuan became a tributary state of Luang Prabang' (no later date on the page: Vietnam under the Nguyễn later annexed Muang Phuan, undated, Kingdom of Vientiane page).

1791: Siam occupies Luang Prabang. The ruler list gives 'Siamese occupation (1791-1792)'; the History of Laos page: 'In 1791, Anuruttha was confirmed by Rama I as king of Luang Prabang' and 'By 1792 Nanthasen had convinced Rama I that Anuruttha was secretly dealing with the Burmese'.
1792: the first Siamese occupation ends; Anurutha reigns 1792-1819.

A second Siamese occupation ('Siamese occupation (179.. - 2 June 1794)'). The page prints the start year as '179..', so 1793 is my placeholder between the first occupation and the end date; confidence 1.
2 June 1794: the second Siamese occupation ends ('Siamese occupation (179.. - 2 June 1794)').

region.text: the Sipsong Chau Tai: Lai Châu, Điện Biên, Sơn La and the upper Black River (Tai Dam and Tai Khao lords)

ledger.note: 7 April 1889: the Sipsong Chau Tai pass to France. The Sipsong Chau Tai 'was incorporated into the French protectorate of Tonkin ... after 1888'; the French 'signed a treaty with Đèo Văn Trị, the White Tai lord of Muang Lay (Lai Châu) on 7 April 1889'. Cliopatria's 1890 shape drops these provinces. The page lists Lan Xang among the powers the Tai lords paid tribute to; whether Luang Prabang's claim was more than tribute is not stated.

region.text: the Luang Prabang kingdom east of the Mekong, ceded by Siam

ledger.note: October 1893: Luang Prabang becomes a French protectorate. 'France and Siam went to war in 1893, culminating in the Paknam incident'; 'Siam was forced to accept the French ultimatum, to cede the lands east of the Mekong'; 'The French Protectorate of Laos was officially established, with the administrative capital moved from Luang Prabang to Vientiane'. Infobox 'Franco-Siamese conflict: 13 July - 3 October 1893'; the protection treaty of 27 March 1889 and the French consulate of 1885 came before. The royal house stayed on until 1947.

wars.name: Burmese-Siamese War (1765-1767)
wars.outcome: Vientiane's Ong Boun wrote to Hsinbyushin in October 1764 'urging the Burmese to invade his rival Luang Prabang'; 'Luang Prabang fell to the Burmese in March 1765' and became a Burmese vassal. No land changed hands.
wars.note: The vassal tint is in the konbaung-dynasty ledger.

wars.name: Lao rebellion (1826-1828)
wars.outcome: 'Anouvong made more direct overtures to Luang Prabang in February 1827,' seeking support and supplies; the page does not say what Luang Prabang did. Siam won and annexed Vientiane.
wars.note: Luang Prabang's land was not touched.

wars.name: Haw wars
wars.outcome: 'A particularly destructive attack during the Haw wars by the Chinese Black Flag Army in 1887' reached Luang Prabang; the French conducted campaigns against the Haw in Laos and Tonkin until the 1880s. No dated change of land on the pages.
wars.note: The History of Laos page: 'The French would increasingly conduct military campaigns against the Haw in Laos and Vietnam (Tonkin) until the 1880s'.

wars.name: Franco-Siamese War (1893)

zones.text: the Luang Prabang kingdom east of the Mekong

wars.outcome: France forced Siam to cede the lands east of the Mekong; Luang Prabang became a French protectorate and the administrative capital of Laos moved to Vientiane.

certainty.note: No treaty or survey line: the borders with Vientiane, Muang Phuan, Burma, Chiang Mai and Tonkin are approximate; the Sipsong Chau Tai and Muang Phuan are tributary margins.

The 1889 French treaty with the White Tai lord of Muang Lay and the 1893 cession of the east bank were fixed by treaty, but the line itself is not given on the pages opened; only the Sipsong Chau Tai frontier is firm.

notes:
Page budget 9; six pages opened (WebFetch summaries, so every quotation is the summariser's quotation). The Luang Prabang page is thin: no area, no boundaries and few dates; the dates for 1707, 1791-1794, 1885-1893 come from it, the rest from the pages of the neighbours.

Cliopatria's thirteen shapes are one outline (Louangphrabang, Oudomxai, Phongsali, Houaphan, Xiangkhouang, Bokeo, Louang Namtha, Xaignabouri and 62 per cent of Vientiane province in Laos, and Lai Chau, Dien Bien, Son La, Lao Cai and Yen Bai in Vietnam) with three changes: a loss of 12,600 km2 in the west in 1783 (Bokeo and Louang Namtha, which Cliopatria's Chiangmai row holds from 1783; no page opened records it; the 1783 shape is marked adjust and restores them at confidence 1, and the chiangmai dossier removes them from its side), a loss of the five Vietnamese provinces in 1890 (the French treaty with Muang Lay is dated 7 April 1889, so the 1885 shape is marked adjust) and the end in 1894. The kingdom became a French protectorate in 1893, so this dossier ends in October 1893; Cliopatria draws no state on the Luang Prabang land in 1894 (French Indochina begins with Laos in 1895): the french-indochina dossier should start Laos in 1894, or this dossier should be extended to 1894 by the reviewer.

Tributaries. Muang Phuan (Xiangkhouang) was a tributary from 1707 on the page but is drawn as direct land; the vassal_start has no matching vassal_end because the pages opened do not date the end (the Kingdom of Vientiane page has Vietnam annexing Muang Phuan after 1828, undated). The Sipsong Chau Tai paid tribute to several powers, including Lan Xang, by the page's words; Cliopatria draws them as Luang Prabang land. Both should be tints, but only Xiangkhouang is dated. Houaphan (Sam Neua) is not mentioned on any page opened.

Suzerains. The Burmese suzerainty of 1765-1778 is in the konbaung-dynasty ledger; the Siamese suzerainty of 1778-1893 (a 'vassal of Siam' status line) should be in the rattanakosin-kingdom/thonburi-kingdom dossiers; this state is the vassal and records no event for it. The page lists Surinyavong II as 'Burmese vassal, 1768-1788' and the status as Siamese from 1778; I read the Siamese line as the later and truer.

Counterparts that need dossiers: muang-phuan (the Plain of Jars principality, tributary of Luang Prabang, Siam and Vietnam), sip-song-chau-tai (the Tai lords of the upper Black River) and the Black Flag Army / Haw bands (rebel, 1860s-1880s).

Names for the gazetteer: none beyond the Natural Earth units used.
